title: Ignatius to the Trallians
subtitle: truly born, truly crucified, truly raised: 'without these it is not called a church'
lead: At Smyrna, on his way under guard to die in Rome, Ignatius of Antioch was visited by Polybius, the overseer of Tralles, a rich city on the road east from Ephesus. He wrote back to the Trallian church. The first half asks it to respect its overseer, elders and deacons, and holds one of the most quoted lines on church order: 'Without these, it is not called a church' (3:1).

The second half warns against teachers who said Christ 'suffered only in appearance' (10:1). Against them Ignatius sets a confession built on one word: Christ 'was truly born, and he ate and drank. He was truly persecuted under Pontius Pilate. He was truly crucified and died' and 'truly raised from the dead' (9:1-2). If not, 'Then I am dying for nothing' (10:1). No church counts the letter as Scripture; it is read here as an early witness, with the New Testament as the measure.
facts: No church. It is not in the New Testament of the Council of Trent (Catholic), the Westminster Confession (Reformed), the Second London Baptist Confession, the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church's list of 35 New Testament books, or the Thirty-Nine Articles' 'Books of the New Testament, as they are commonly received'.
Ignatius, overseer of the church at Antioch in Syria, on his way to execution in Rome. Eusebius names the letter, to the church 'in Tralles, whose ruler then was Polybius' (Church History 3.36.5).

Written at Smyrna (12:1) on the journey to Rome. Undated; To the Romans, written there too, ends 'I write this to you on the 24th of August' in Lake's English (Ignatius to the Romans 10:3); Lightfoot gives the day as 'August 23rd'. Lake: in his Chronicle Eusebius fixes the martyrdom 'in the tenth year of Trajan, i.e. 108 A.D.', and there is 'a general tendency to think that Ignatius was really a martyr in Rome in the time of Trajan (98-117 A.D.)'.
Smyrna, with the churches of God present there (12:1)
The church at Tralles in the Roman province of Asia, with its overseer Polybius, its council of elders and its deacons (1:1; 2:2-3)
Letter of thanks and warning from a condemned prisoner
Kirsopp Lake's Greek (Loeb, 1912), the short (middle) recension: the Medicean manuscript at Florence (G), the long recension (g), and the Latin (L), Armenian (A) and Syriac (S) versions.
authorship: The letter claims to be by 'Ignatius, also called Theophorus' (1:0), a prisoner (1:1; 10:1; 12:2) whose church is in Syria (13:1). Eusebius knew it as one of the four letters written at Smyrna and names Polybius (Church History 3.36.5). Lightfoot: it seems probable that Polybius and the others named 'were not fictitious personages'.

The seven letters survive in three forms: a long recension with interpolations and added letters, the short (middle) recension of the seven Eusebius names, which Lake follows, and a Syriac abridgment of three letters that does not include To the Trallians (Lake). In 1910 the Catholic Encyclopedia wrote: 'While it can hardly be said that there is at present any unanimous agreement on the subject, the best modern criticism favors the authenticity of the seven letters mentioned by Eusebius'. Later in the twentieth century the question was opened again: Sergio Zañartu's survey (Teología y Vida, 2009) names R. Weijenborg (1969), R. Joly (1979), J. Rius-Camps (1980), R. M. Hübner (1997) and T. Lechner (1999) among those who argued that the letters, or some of them, are later; Zañartu himself holds to the short recension's authenticity until the contrary is proved. B. A. Zuiddam (Ekklesiastikos Pharos, 2010) argues that the seven-letter text may be a medieval abridgment. Fritz Guy (1964) wrote that 'The conclusions of Zahn and Lightfoot have since been accepted by practically all scholars'.

audience.to: The church at Tralles, a wealthy city of the Roman province of Asia on the high road from Ephesus to the East (Lightfoot), whose overseer Polybius had come to Ignatius at Smyrna (1:1). It had a council of elders and deacons (2:2-3), lived already in the order Ignatius asks for ('as you already do', 2:2), and had not, so far as Ignatius knew, taken up the teaching he warns against (8:1).
audience.why: To thank the church for its overseer's visit, to confirm it in respect for the overseer, elders and deacons (2-3; 7; 12-13), and above all to guard it in advance against teachers who said Christ suffered only in appearance (6-11). Lightfoot: 'The main purport of the letter is a warning against the poison of Docetism'. Knowing that the Trallians had not yet met the teaching explains why the warnings come with praise.
views: Lake: 'docetism (δοκεῖν), which regarded the sufferings, and in some cases the life, of Jesus as merely an appearance'; whether the Judaizing tendency of the other letters belonged to the same circles 'is disputed'. Lightfoot: no allusion is made here 'to the Judaic side of the heresy', but a comparison with the other letters shows 'these false teachers to have been Judaizers also'.

outline: Greeting to the church in Tralles
Subject to the overseer; deacons of the mysteries
Without these it is not called a church
The foreign weed; poison in honeyed wine
Faith the flesh, love the blood
Truly born, truly crucified, truly raised
Greetings from Smyrna; my chains urge you

lenses.name: Historical-critical
lenses.desc: Reads the letter as a source: Tralles and Polybius, who the opponents were and whether they are the same as the 'Judaism' of Magnesians, and the corrupt places (3:3; 6:2; 7:1).

lenses.name: New Testament
lenses.desc: Follows the New Testament in the letter: 1 Corinthians 4:1 and Acts 6 on deacons, 1 Corinthians 3:1-2 on infants, Colossians 1:16 on the unseen powers, Philippians 2:10 and 1 Corinthians 15 in the confession, Matthew 15:13, Isaiah 52:5 and Romans 2:24, 1 John 4:2-3 on Christ come in the flesh.

lenses.name: Church order and the churches
lenses.desc: Reads the letter for the questions churches still ask of it: overseer, elders and deacons (2-3; 7:2; 12:2), 'without these it is not called a church' (3:1), and deacons not 'of food and drink' (2:3), each church's reading from its own documents.

sections.b: Eusebius: at Smyrna Ignatius wrote to Ephesus, to Magnesia, 'and another to the one in Tralles, whose ruler then was Polybius, he records' (Church History 3.36.5). Lightfoot follows Strabo's road: 'After leaving Magnesia the road leads to Tralles'. Ephesus and Magnesia sent several delegates; Tralles, 'as being more distant, was content with sending a single representative, its bishop Polybius' (Lightfoot). In him Ignatius saw 'your whole congregation' (1:1).

The deacons are 'deacons of the mysteries of Jesus Christ', 'not deacons of food and drink' (2:3); all are to respect the deacons 'as Jesus Christ', the overseer as 'a type of the Father', the elders 'as God's council and as the band of the apostles': 'Without these, it is not called a church' (3:1). The Catechism of the Catholic Church quotes the verse (1549; 1554). The Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran, Reformed and Baptist documents in the views note at 3:1 do not discuss Ignatius; they give each church's own answer to what makes a church. Lightfoot called the letters' language 'this extravagant exaltation of the episcopal office', with 'the extenuating fact' that 'the needs and distractions of the age seemed to call for a greater concentration of authority in the episcopate'.

Chapters 6-11 are the center. The teachers mix Christ into their teaching 'to win trust', like poisoners with honeyed wine (6:2). Ignatius answers with a confession in which 'truly' comes four times (9:1-2), and with his own chains: if Christ 'suffered only in appearance', 'Then I am dying for nothing' (10:1). Lightfoot: 'The denunciation of Docetism is fuller and more explicit in this than in any other of his letters.' See the topics Docetism and The Incarnation.

The text rests on one Greek manuscript (G) with the long recension and the versions, and Lake and Lightfoot mend G in many places from them. Lake calls 3:3 'confused and corrupt in all the authorities' and 6:2 'clearly corrupt'; at 7:1 'The text is doubtful' (the Armenian lacks 'God'). G reads 'flesh and blood' for 'flesh and spirit' (1:0), 'Son of the Father' for 'type of the Father' (3:1), and leaves out 'but whoever is outside the altar is not pure' (7:2). At 12:3 Lightfoot calls the verb 'obviously corrupt' and prints Bunsen's emendation. The Plain English Translation follows Lake's printed text in each place, and the variants give the other readings.

spec.title: Claude's theory: the gentle overseer and the gentle prisoner
spec.body: The letter praises Polybius's gentleness ('his gentleness is power', 3:2), then says Ignatius himself needs gentleness, 'by which the ruler of this age is brought down' (4:2), and asks the church to 'take up a gentle spirit' (8:1). The teachers, by contrast, are sweet only on the surface, like honeyed wine with poison in it (6:2). I suggest the letter sets two kinds of softness against each other: the overseer's real gentleness, which is power, and the teachers' false sweetness, which is death.

Style: sketched by hand onto an old rolled parchment scroll. canon.summary: Ignatius to the Trallians is an early Christian letter in no church's Bible. Its author, the martyr Ignatius of Antioch, is honored by the Catholic and Orthodox churches, the Church of England and a district of the Lutheran Church—Missouri Synod, and the Catholic Catechism quotes this letter on the bishop and the three orders (1549; 1554).
accepted_by: Not Scripture: the Council of Trent's list of New Testament books (1546) does not include it. The U.S. bishops' calendar keeps 17 October as the Memorial of 'Saint Ignatius of Antioch, Bishop and Martyr'. The Catechism quotes 3:1 at 1549 and in full at 1554.

Not part of the Bible: Reid (1908) states that the Eastern Orthodox churches 'have a New Testament identical with the Catholic'. The Orthodox Church in America commemorates 'Hieromartyr Ignatius the God-Bearer, Bishop of Antioch' on 20 December.
Not Scripture: the church's list of 35 New Testament books, which adds eight books to the 27, among them 'The book of Clement' and the 'Didascalia', does not name it.

Not Scripture: Article VI receives 'All the Books of the New Testament, as they are commonly received'. The Church of England's Common Worship calendar keeps 17 October as a Lesser Festival of 'Ignatius, Bishop of Antioch, Martyr, c.107'.

The calendar of the church's Southern District commemorates 'Ignatius of Antioch, Pastor and Martyr' on 17 October, and says he 'was the first to use the word catholic to describe the universality of the Church'. That is a district page; the synod's own calendar was not opened.
Not Scripture: the Westminster Confession lists the 27 books of the New Testament as 'all the books of the Old and New Testaments, which are these'.
Not Scripture: the Second London Baptist Confession (1689) lists the same 27 books, 'All of which are given by the inspiration of God, to be the rule of faith and life'.

provenance.h: Smyrna, on the way to Rome
provenance.b: Ignatius wrote at Smyrna (12:1), after Polybius, the overseer of Tralles, visited him there (1:1). Eusebius lists it third of the four letters from Smyrna and names Polybius as the church's 'ruler then' (Church History 3.36.5).

In the Greek Medicean manuscript at Florence (G), in the long recension (g), and in Latin (L), Armenian (A) and Syriac (S) versions (Lake). The Syriac abridgment of three letters does not include it (Lake). At 3:3 and 6:2 all the witnesses are damaged; there and in several other places (1:0; 3:1; 7:2) Lake prints the Greek manuscript mended from the long recension and the versions (see the variants).

rejected_why.h: A bishop's letter, not an apostle's
rejected_why.b: The early church received into the New Testament writings it held to come from the apostles and their circle. Ignatius says so himself: he did not think that 'I, a condemned man, should give you orders like an apostle' (3:3).

rejected_why.h: Treated as a letter of a church writer
rejected_why.b: Eusebius describes the letters in his history (Church History 3.36) and does not mention Ignatius in his survey of the books accepted, disputed and rejected for the New Testament (Church History 3.25).

cited_in.b: 'Those in heaven, on earth and under the earth': the same three Greek words. The New Testament does not quote this letter.
The plant not planted by the Father, in Lake's margin; Ignatius uses the same word phyteia.
John's test of confessing Christ 'come in the flesh' is the issue of 9-10.
The name blasphemed among the nations (Lake's margin; quoted by Romans 2:24), in Ignatius's own form.

reliability.verdict: This is Claude's analysis, not a church's judgment. As a witness to Christian belief in Asia early in the second century the letter is of the first importance: the fullest of Ignatius's confessions against the teaching that Christ only seemed to suffer, a church with one overseer, elders and deacons, and the much-quoted 'Without these, it is not called a church'. Its text rests on one medieval Greek manuscript with the long recension and versions; it is corrupt at 3:3 and 6:2, and the manuscript goes wrong elsewhere too (1:0; 3:1; 7:2). Its historical claims are few and fit Eusebius. On Christ it follows the New Testament closely; its claims for the offices go beyond it.

sections.h: 1. As a witness to early Christian belief
sections.b: High. The letter shows a church ordered under an overseer, elders and deacons, with deacons whose work is more than serving food (2:3); a confession of Christ's birth, eating and drinking, suffering under Pontius Pilate, death and resurrection, each 'truly' (9:1-2); and teachers who said he suffered 'only in appearance' (10:1).

Fair. One Greek manuscript of the short recension survives, with Latin, Armenian and Syriac versions. Lake calls 3:3 'confused and corrupt in all the authorities' and 6:2 'clearly corrupt'; at 7:1 'the text is doubtful'. The Greek manuscript also reads 'Son of the Father' at 3:1 and leaves out a clause at 7:2 (Lightfoot). The Plain English Translation follows Lake and gives the readings in the variants.

The letter claims to be by Ignatius, writing from Smyrna (12:1), and names Polybius (1:1). Eusebius knew it and names Polybius (Church History 3.36.5). The genuineness of the seven letters was long debated, and the debate was renewed in the twentieth century: the authorship section gives the views and who holds them.

Matches: Christ of David's line (9:1; Romans 1:3), born of a woman (Galatians 4:4), eating and drinking (Acts 10:41), suffering under Pontius Pilate (1 Timothy 6:13), raised by the Father, who will raise believers (9:2; 1 Corinthians 15:12-20); the test of Christ 'come in the flesh' (10:1; 1 John 4:2); the plant the Father did not plant (11:1; Matthew 15:13); the church as Christ's body (11:2; Colossians 1:18). Goes beyond: 'Without these, it is not called a church' (3:1) and 'whoever does anything without the overseer, the council of elders and the deacons is not pure in his conscience' (7:2) have no parallel in the New Testament, where the elders of Ephesus are called overseers (Acts 20:17, 28); churches read this difference in different ways (see the views note at 3:1 and the cards on bishops). Conflicts: none on a point of doctrine.

how_to_read.b: Read 1-5 (order and humility), 6-11 (the warning and the confession) and 12-13 (greetings). The order of the church is offered as the guard against the false teaching.
At 1:0, 3:1, 3:3, 6:2, 7:1, 7:2 and 12:2-3 the witnesses differ or are corrupt; read the variant entries before building on those verses.

how_to_read.h: As a witness the churches read differently
how_to_read.b: Catholic teaching quotes 3:1 (Catechism 1549; 1554). The views note at 3:1 sets the other churches' own statements on what makes a church beside it; they do not discuss Ignatius.
